links.outcome: Discrimination of recalibrated CSO vs existing JHFRAT and XGBoost benchmark against proxy labels
links.effect: CSO AUC-ROC 0.91 vs JHFRAT 0.86 (augmented); XGBoost higher at 0.96; augmented CSO sensitivity at threshold 13 was 0.57 vs 0.29 for JHFRAT.
links.quote: The CSO model demonstrated significant improvements over the current JHFRAT in classification alignment with the proxy labels (CSO AUC-ROC = 0.91, JHFRAT AUC-ROC = 0.86).

links.outcome: Whether retuning JHFRAT item weights on local data improves classification at existing thresholds
links.effect: Recalibrated CSO correctly reclassified 3,788 high-risk patients (27%) from moderate/low categories; 860 low-risk (4.2%) correctly downgraded; 264 (1.3%) low-risk reclassified as high-risk.
links.quote: Our augmented CSO model correctly reclassified 3,788 high-risk patients (27% of the high-risk cohort) from moderate- or low-risk categories.

links.outcome: Limitations on validation data representativeness and generalizability
links.effect: Study used only three hospitals in one health system, with cohort exclusions by length of stay and data availability that may inflate performance; no external validation.
links.quote: The systematic exclusion of encounters based on JHFRAT data availability and length of stay introduces biases to the study cohort by reducing patient heterogeneity in the model training and validation, potentially inflating model performance.

links.outcome: Reference standard validity using proxy labels from nurse intervention patterns
links.effect: Labels derived from clinician interventions rather than true fall risk introduce confounding by indication and endogeneity; models benefit from this, and gains may be smaller for actual fall prediction.
links.quote: By design, the JHFRAT scores influence intervention decisions, and therefore the intervention-based labels introduce endogeneity from which our models benefit.

links.outcome: Stability of model feature importances under variation in labeling rules (sensitivity analysis)
links.effect: CSO feature importances remained stable as fall-encounter weighting increased (largest variation 4.39 percentage points), while XGBoost importances varied more substantially (e.g., requires assistance 14.00–25.81%).
links.quote: The constrained score optimization feature importances remain stable as the weighting of fall encounters increases, while the XGBoost feature importances vary more substantially.

links.outcome: Whether interpretable score-based model retains clinical usability versus black-box XGBoost
links.effect: CSO trades some AUC for a score retaining meaning on the JHFRAT scale, whereas projected XGBoost scores distribute to unrealistic extremes and lose interpretive meaning.
links.quote: Without score clipping, projected XGBoost risk scores distribute to unrealistic extremes on the JHFRAT scale and lose interpretive meaning.
